Name: Three Pecks of Knights' Gold Rings Before the Carthaginian Council of One Hundred, and a Rebuff
RagShortTexts: In 216 BC Mago Barca returned to the Carthaginian Senate under orders, bearing the news of the great victory at Cannae
In the hall of the Council of One Hundred he poured out three pecks of gold rings stripped from the bodies of Roman knights
He urged full reinforcement of Italy but met mockery and obstruction from the oligarchic faction of Hanno the Great
BaseText: In 216 BC, after the Battle of Cannae, Hannibal's youngest brother Mago Barca returned to Carthage on Hannibal's orders to report the victory to the Council of One Hundred. In the middle of the Senate's assembly hall, Mago had his attendants pour out on the stone steps, before everyone, three full pecks (about one bushel) of pure gold signet rings stripped from the fingers of fallen Roman knights and nobles. The gold glittered and the clash of rings rang out like thunder, and the hall burst into uproar. Mago seized the moment to demand more infantry, cavalry, elephants and money for a final blow. But the faction leader Hanno the Great sneered and attacked him on the spot, asking: 'If Hannibal has truly destroyed the enemy as his report says, why does he still ask the homeland for reinforcements and supplies? If Rome is suing for peace, where are its envoys?' Obstructed by the conservative merchant oligarchs, the reinforcements were delayed again and again, and in the end the chance of a lifetime to crush Rome for good was lost.

Variants.Content: Those three pecks of gold rings were cast from the corpses of Roman nobles! The soldiers at the front bled to win all of Italy, yet these merchants sitting in ivory chairs cannot bear to part with a single silver coin!

The madmen of the Barca family only want to pour the city's hard-earned money into the bottomless pit of Italy! What are a few looted rings worth? Rome still has not surrendered, so why should we go bankrupt for his ambition!
The gods have filled the enemy's council with envy and blindness. The selfishness and infighting of the Carthaginians are the strongest shield protecting the Roman Republic.
